title: Act IV, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern ask Hamlet where the body is. He mocks Rosencrantz as a sponge and answers in riddles, then runs off.

vocabulary.context: I am glad of it: a knavish speech sleeps in a foolish ear.
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Hamlet (2026-10-20)

etymology.checked: 2026-10-21 (language, form and meaning taken from the Wiktionary entry's etymology templates; wording ours)

context.history: Sponges soak and are squeezed dry.

discussionQuestions: Where does characterization appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with death and mortality?

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act IV, Scene II develops the idea of Hamlet hides the body. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act IV, Scene II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Hamlet hides the body. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act IV, Scene II suggests about Hamlet hides the body. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act IV, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of Hamlet hides the body. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act IV, Scene II within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Hamlet hides the body responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act IV, Scene II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Hamlet hides the body follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act IV, Scene II and its treatment of Hamlet hides the body. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act IV, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about Hamlet hides the body in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act IV, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Hamlet hides the body. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Hamlet exposes Rosencrantz as a tool. Useful evidence: “Ay, sir, that soaks up the king’s countenance” (Act IV, Scene II, Hamlet (speech 11)): Rosencrantz as sponge. On diction / vocabulary: "The body is with the king, but the king is not with the body." Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
